FOR FAMILIES HIRING AN ESTATE SALE COMPANY

A lower headline rate is not always the better quote.

Estate sale companies usually price on a tiered commission schedule — a higher rate on the first few thousand dollars, a lower rate above it — plus separate setup, card-processing, and haul-away fees a single percentage does not include. Enter a company's actual schedule against your estimated sale total to see the real net proceeds, and compare two quotes side by side.

Estimated sale and Company A's quote

Enter the commission tiers as the company quoted them. If a company charges one flat rate, put it in Tier 1 and set the Tier 1 threshold at or above your estimated sale total.

Compare against a second company's quote

Same estimated sale total as above, this company's own tiers and fees.

        Common questions

        Why isn't a single commission percentage enough to compare estate sale quotes?

        Most estate sale companies price on a tiered schedule -- a higher rate on the first few thousand dollars of sales, a lower rate above that -- plus separate flat fees for setup/staging, credit-card processing, and hauling away or donating unsold items. Two quotes that both mention "30%" can settle very differently once their tiers and fees are applied to the same estimated sale total. This calculator applies each company's actual schedule rather than a single headline rate.

        What is a minimum guarantee?

        Some contracts promise the family a minimum payout no matter how the sale actually goes. If you enter one, this calculator floors the settlement at that amount whenever the computed commission-and-fees math would leave less. Whether that guarantee is actually binding depends on the contract's own wording -- this tool only applies the number you give it.

        Does this replace reading the actual contract?

        No. This is a worksheet for comparing quotes before you sign, built from the numbers you enter. The company's written contract is what actually governs the sale -- read it, and ask the company to explain any fee or tier this calculator doesn't have a field for.

        Is my data uploaded anywhere?

        No. All arithmetic runs in your browser. Sale estimates, commission rates, and settlement figures are never uploaded or sent to a server. The optional usage counter records only which features were used and the day, never any of your numbers.

        Still working from the percentages each company quoted you? Read this calculator vs. comparing headline commission rates — it works through a $12,000 sale where the company quoting the lowest rate keeps the larger share.

        Working with a smaller or more modest estate? Read why estate sale fees bite harder on a smaller sale — the same flat fee stack that's 7.92% of a $12,000 sale is 47.50% of a $2,000 one.

        No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not legal, tax, financial, or estate-planning advice, and it does not replace a qualified professional or the estate sale company's own written contract. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

        Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record.

        Everything runs in your browser. Sale estimates, commission rates, and settlement figures are never uploaded and never appear in a usage count — those are anonymous tallies of which features were used, stored locally. We don't have accounts, tracking cookies, or an analytics vendor.

        Not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by any specific estate sale company. This tool computes against the numbers you enter from your own quotes; it does not look up or verify any company's actual pricing.

        Free and open source. If it helps you compare a quote, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

vs-headline-commission-rate.html.text:
← back to the calculator

This calculator vs. comparing headline commission rates

Gathering two or three estate sale quotes is the standard advice, and the usual next step is to line up the percentages: 30% against 35%, take the lower one. That works when both companies charge one flat rate and nothing else. It stops working as soon as a schedule has tiers or the contract has flat fees — and most do both, which is how the company quoting the smallest number ends up keeping the larger share.

What each one is for

A headline commission rate is a real term from the contract and a fair way to start the conversation. What it cannot do is stand for the contract. A tiered schedule charges its highest rate on the first dollars of the sale, so the low tier a company leads with may apply only to the top slice — or, on a smaller sale, to nothing at all. And a headline rate describes commission only: setup or staging, credit-card processing, and haul-away or donation fees come off on top of it without moving any percentage in the schedule.

This calculator applies each company's actual tier schedule and each of its flat fees to the same estimated gross sale, applies a minimum guarantee if the contract has one, and reports what the family actually takes home — alongside total retained, the single percentage a headline rate was trying to be.

QuestionWhere to answer it
Roughly what do estate sale companies charge?Either one — headline rates are a fine way to get oriented before you have written quotes.
Of these two written quotes, which nets my family more?This calculator — it is the question a pair of headline rates cannot answer once tiers or fees are involved.
What is this company keeping in total, not just in commission?This calculator's total-retained figure, which includes every flat fee.
Does the answer change if the sale brings in less than we hope?This calculator — re-run it at a lower gross estimate; tier thresholds can reverse the result.
Is anything I enter uploaded anywhere?No. The calculator runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent to a server.

A worked example where the headline rate points the wrong way

Two quotes against the same $12,000 estimated gross sale. Company A leads with “25% above $8,000” — the lowest percentage either company says out loud. Company B quotes a flat 35% and charges nothing else.

Company ACompany B
Headline rate quoted25% above $8,00035% flat
Tier schedule40% to $2,000, 30% to $8,000, 25% above35% throughout
Commission$3,600.00$4,200.00
Setup / staging, card processing, haul-away$950.00$0.00
Net to the family$7,450.00$7,800.00
Total retained by the company37.92%35.00%

Company A wins on commission and on every percentage it quoted, and still leaves the family $350 worse off. Its 25% tier only reaches the $4,000 above the threshold; the 40% tier takes the first $2,000 regardless; and the $950 of flat fees appears in no rate at all. Comparing the two headline numbers — 25% against 35% — gets this backwards.

These figures come from the same module the calculator itself uses, run on the inputs above. They illustrate how the arithmetic behaves; they are not a claim about any real company's pricing. Your own quotes will differ, which is the reason to enter them.

Common questions

What is a headline commission rate?

The single percentage a company leads with when asked what it charges — “we're 30%”, or “25% over $8,000”. It is a real number from the contract, but it is one number out of a schedule that usually has two or three, and it describes commission only. The flat fees are quoted separately or further down the page.

Why can the company with the lower headline rate cost more?

Two reasons stack. A tiered schedule charges its highest rate on the first dollars of the sale, so the low tier a company leads with may only apply to the top slice — on a smaller sale it may never apply at all. And setup or staging, credit-card processing, and haul-away or donation fees are deducted on top of commission, so they raise the share retained without changing any percentage in the schedule.

Is a headline rate ever enough to compare on?

Yes, when both companies quote one flat rate across the whole sale and neither adds flat fees. Then the headline rate is the whole contract and the lower one nets more. That is the case this calculator agrees with you about in a few seconds — the point is that you find out which case you are in rather than assuming it.

What does “total retained” mean here?

Commission plus every flat fee, expressed as a share of the estimated gross sale. It is the number a headline rate is standing in for: what the company keeps in total, as one percentage you can hold next to another company's. It is computed from the schedule and fees you enter, so it changes with your estimated sale total.

Do I need exact numbers from the contracts?

Enter what the written quotes say and treat the result as a planning estimate. The gross sale total is an estimate by nature, and the tiers interact with it — a schedule that looks better at $8,000 can look worse at $20,000, so it is worth re-running at a high and a low estimate rather than one figure.

Is anything I enter uploaded anywhere?

No. The calculator this page links to runs entirely in your browser; nothing you enter about either company's quote is uploaded.

No warranty. This page and the linked calculator produce planning estimates from numbers you supply. They are not legal, tax, financial, or estate-planning advice, and they do not replace a qualified professional or either company's written contract. You are responsible for verifying anything here against the quotes and contracts you were actually given. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Nothing leaves your browser. The calculator this page links to runs entirely client-side; nothing you enter is uploaded anywhere.

Nothing here says or implies that quoting a headline rate is dishonest, or that a tiered schedule is worse than a flat one. A headline rate is a summary, and the point of this page is only that a summary is not what you should sign against.

why-estate-sale-fees-bite-harder-on-a-sm.text:
← back to the calculator

Why estate sale fees bite harder on a smaller sale

The same contract, applied to the same household's own numbers, can retain a very different share depending on how large the sale turns out to be. Run one company's schedule against a $12,000, a $4,000, and a $2,000 estimated sale and the total retained goes 37.92% → 58.75% → 87.50% — not because the contract changed, but because a flat fee stack does not shrink with the sale and a tiered commission charges its highest rate first.

One schedule, three sale sizes

Same company throughout: 40% commission on the first $2,000 of sales, 30% on the next $6,000, 25% above that, plus a flat $400 setup/staging fee, $250 credit-card processing fee, and $300 haul-away/donation fee — $950 in flat fees regardless of sale size.

Estimated gross saleCommission-only rateFlat fees as % of saleTotal retainedFamily nets
$12,00030.00%7.92%37.92%$7,450.00
$4,00035.00%23.75%58.75%$1,650.00
$2,00040.00%47.50%87.50%$250.00

Figures computed by this calculator's own shipped arithmetic, not estimated for this page.

Two effects, both pointing the same way

The commission tiers front-load the highest rate. The 40% tier only covers the first $2,000 of any sale, so a $2,000 sale never reaches the cheaper 30% or 25% tiers at all — its blended commission-only rate is a full 40.00%. A $12,000 sale spreads far enough into the 25% tier that its blended rate drops to 30.00%, even though every dollar is priced from the identical schedule.

The flat fees do not move with the sale. $950 in setup, processing, and haul-away fees is a fixed cost of running the sale at all — it is 7.92% of a $12,000 sale and 47.50% of a $2,000 sale, the same dollars measured against very different totals.

Together they mean the household with the smaller estate loses the larger share of it, from the same written contract a larger estate would sign.

What to do with this before signing

Run the company's actual schedule against your own estimated gross sale total, not a round number from the conversation — the calculator this page links to does the tier and fee arithmetic for you. If the estimate is uncertain, as it usually is before the sale happens, run it at both a low and a high estimate; a contract that looks reasonable at $12,000 can retain most of a $2,000 sale under the same terms. If the flat-fee stack looks large relative to your estimate, that is a specific, answerable question to put to the company before you sign — not a reason to assume anything improper, since setup, processing, and disposal are real costs the company incurs whatever the sale total turns out to be.

Common questions

Why do estate sale fees take a bigger share of a smaller sale?

Because setup/staging, credit-card processing, and haul-away/donation fees are usually flat dollar amounts, not percentages. A $950 fee stack is a fixed cost regardless of whether the sale brings in $12,000 or $2,000, so it is 7.92% of the larger sale and 47.50% of the smaller one — the same dollars, a much bigger share of a smaller household.

Does the commission rate also change with sale size?

Yes, in the opposite direction from what a headline rate suggests. A tiered schedule (for example 40% on the first $2,000, 30% on the next $6,000, 25% above that) charges its highest rate on the first dollars of any sale, so the blended commission-only percentage falls as the sale gets larger: 40.00% on a $2,000 sale, 35.00% on a $4,000 sale, 30.00% on a $12,000 sale in this calculator's own worked example — before the flat fees are even added.

So does total retained rise or fall as a sale gets smaller?

It rises, and both effects push the same direction: the commission tiers charge their highest rate first, and the flat fees do not shrink with the sale. On this calculator's own worked example, the same company's schedule and $950 fee stack retains 37.92% of a $12,000 sale, 58.75% of a $4,000 sale, and 87.50% of a $2,000 sale.

What does this mean for a small or modest estate?

That the flat-fee stack is worth asking about directly, not just the commission percentage — and that a company's schedule is worth running against your own estimated sale total rather than a round number from a conversation, since the same contract can retain very different shares depending on how large the sale actually is.
